strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel formulation: casting horizon-aware betting for anytime-valid tests as a finite-horizon optimal control/dynamic-programming problem over the state (t, log W_t). This is a clean and useful lens that had not been previously applied to this problem (the only prior horizon-aware work, STaR-Bets, uses a different construction).

The theoretical contributions (Theorem 3.1 and Propositions 3.4/3.6) are rigorous and give genuine qualitative insight: (i) in an interior 'tubular' region, deviating from Kelly is provably costly via a clean martingale/Hoeffding argument; (ii) sufficient conditions via Sanov-type large-deviation rate functions formalize when aggressive betting helps when 'behind schedule' and defensive betting helps when 'ahead of schedule'. The proofs are carefully worked out in the appendix (including a technical type-quantization lemma, Lemma A.3, handling the transition from continuous to finite-alphabet rate functions).

The resulting three-regime 'phase diagram' is a nice unifying narrative that connects the theory to a concrete, interpretable action space for the proposed DQN, giving the RL method a principled inductive bias rather than being a black-box heuristic.

The DQN is designed to preserve anytime-validity exactly by construction (bets are always clipped into the valid range and features are strictly predictable/F_{t-1}-measurable), so the learning-based approach does not sacrifice the core statistical guarantee — an important and correctly-handled point.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: deadline-limited power curves, learned modal-action maps that qualitatively match the oracle DP phase diagrams (Figure 2 vs Figure 3), confidence-sequence width comparisons (Figure 4), and CDF-of-lower-confidence-bound comparisons (Figure 5) across a range of Beta/Beta-mixture distributions and deadlines, compared against the current best-known horizon-aware baseline (STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding) as well as sensible heuristic baselines (hedged epsilon-schedules, linear-epsilon).
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with algorithmic pseudocode-level implementation details, full hyperparameter table, feature construction, and training distribution specification.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are only sufficient conditions in specific or restrictive settings (constant-bet policies, finite-alphabet distributions for Propositions 3.4/3.6, or the 'interior tubular region' assumption for Theorem 3.1); the paper does not, and states it cannot, characterize the actual optimal policy in general. The 'phase diagram' is therefore explicitly described as informal/qualitative, and the leap from these partial theoretical results to the specific 3-action DQN design is heuristic rather than derived.

The DQN action space is restricted to only three discrete actions (half empirical-Kelly, empirical-Kelly, all-in/endpoint bet), which is a strong simplification relative to the continuous bet space Λ_m and to the richer discretization used in the oracle DP (which itself only used 3 actions as well, so the 'phase diagram' validation is somewhat circular — the oracle DP was solved with the same restricted action set that the DQN is then shown to recover).

The comparison to the main competing method (STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding) required an ad hoc extension from the one-sided setting (for which STaR was designed and analyzed) to the two-sided setting via a sign-based heuristic (Appendix D). This adaptation is not validated or justified theoretically and could plausibly disadvantage the baseline, which weakens the strength of the head-to-head comparison claims of 'state-of-the-art' performance.

The empirical gains shown in Figures 3–5 are sometimes fairly modest (e.g., the CDF curves for lower confidence bounds in Figure 5(b) are close between DQN and competitors), and the presented results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance assessment despite reporting differences based on Monte Carlo simulation with finite (5000) repetitions.

All experiments (both training and evaluation) are restricted to the Beta and Beta-mixture family of distributions. Although the DQN is called 'universal', its actual demonstrated generalization is only within this fairly narrow, unimodal-friendly family; the paper explicitly defers testing on qualitatively different distributions (e.g., discrete, heavy-tailed, or multimodal beyond the 2-component Beta mixture) to future work, which limits confidence in the claimed generality of the learned policy.

The reliance throughout (both in the heuristics and DQN features) on the predictable empirical Kelly estimate λ̂_t(m) introduces estimation noise that is not accounted for in the theoretical analysis (which assumes knowledge of the population Kelly bet); the interplay between estimation error and the theoretical phase-diagram regions is not analyzed, though it is acknowledged qualitatively (e.g., 'aggressive actions early on...may be undesirable').

No computational cost/complexity comparison is provided among methods (e.g., training cost of the universal DQN, which takes ~3 hours on a GPU and 500k episodes, versus the closed-form or lightweight STaR/heuristic methods), which is relevant for assessing practical significance of the proposed learning-based approach.

strengths: The paper introduces a conceptually appealing reformulation of horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon stochastic control problem in the (t, log W_t) plane, which gives a principled lens (Bellman recursion, Eq. 2) that is new relative to prior horizon-aware betting work (e.g., Voráček & Orabona 2025).

Theorem 3.1 (interior 'tubular' region suboptimality of deviating from Kelly) is a reasonably clean and rigorously proved martingale-concentration result, and the accompanying Example 3.3 gives concrete, checkable numbers that make the abstract conditions tangible.

Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 provide intuitive, information-theoretic (Sanov-type) sufficient conditions explaining when aggressive or defensive betting can beat Kelly when behind/ahead of schedule, nicely matching intuition and validated with worked numerical examples.

The oracle phase-diagrams (Figure 2, via exact Bellman backward induction for a 3-action grid) are a useful sanity check that qualitatively supports the theoretical story and shows how regime boundaries shift with problem difficulty.

Combining the phase-diagram intuition with a practical DQN agent is a reasonable and relatively novel engineering contribution; the use of only predictable (F_{t-1}-measurable) features preserves anytime-validity by construction, which is an important methodological safeguard.

The empirical study is fairly broad in its coverage of diagnostics (deadline-limited power curves, confidence-sequence widths, empirical CDFs of lower confidence bounds) and includes a non-trivial, carefully constructed two-sided adaptation of the STaR baseline for fair comparison.

The appendix is thorough: full proofs, explicit constants, hyperparameter tables, and additional qualitative trajectory plots, which aids reproducibility to a degree uncommon in similarly themed workshop/short papers.
weaknesses: The link between the formal theory (Theorems/Propositions 3.1, 3.4, 3.6) and the headline 'phase diagram' (Figure 1) is loose: the propositions only compare *constant*-bet policies held for the entire remaining horizon T against Kelly, whereas the DQN and the oracle DP policy are explicitly *state-dependent, switching* policies. The paper does not establish that these sufficient conditions for constant policies actually characterize when the truly optimal adaptive policy deviates from Kelly, so the 'phase diagram' remains an informal heuristic rather than a proven structural result, despite language in the abstract/conclusion ('provably suboptimal', 'sufficient conditions') that may oversell this connection.

The sufficient conditions in Propositions 3.4/3.6 are restricted to finite-support distributions and rely on fairly loose, conservative large-deviation (Sanov/typed) bounds with non-vanishing finite-T correction terms; it is unclear how tight or practically informative these conditions are outside the constructed toy examples (Bernoulli with specific p, m).

All empirical validation is synthetic and confined to Beta/Beta-mixture families essentially matching the DQN's own training distribution family (Beta and Beta-mixtures with randomized concentration), which raises concern about the 'universal' claim: the DQN has arguably not been tested outside its training support (e.g., heavy-tailed, discrete, or genuinely out-of-family distributions), despite the paper's own admission that 'exploring its performance on other distributions is an interesting direction for future work.'

The state representation fed to the DQN is a 22-dimensional hand-crafted feature vector that already includes the empirical Kelly estimate, an endpoint/all-in bet, and several derived growth-rate/SNR proxies essentially mirroring the quantities used to define the phase diagram itself; this makes the 'learning' contribution less a discovery of structure from raw data and more a calibration of a policy given features that already encode much of the solution, somewhat undercutting the novelty/significance of the learned result.

The DQN action space is restricted to only 3 discrete actions (half-Kelly, Kelly, all-in), a coarse discretization that does not reflect the continuous λ ∈ Λ_m action space used in the theory and oracle DP; no ablation is given on sensitivity to this choice or comparison with a continuous-action RL approach (e.g., continuous DDPG/SAC variants).

Empirical comparisons lack any measure of statistical uncertainty (error bars, confidence bands, or significance tests) on the reported rejection-probability curves and CS widths (Figures 3–5), making it difficult to assess whether the reported DQN improvements over STaR-Bets/Hedge-over-ε-schedules are robust or within simulation noise, especially since differences in some panels (e.g., Fig. 4b, 5c) appear modest.

Baselines beyond STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding are all constructed by the authors themselves (Linear-ε, Hedge over ε-schedules) rather than adopted from prior literature, and the only external SOTA comparator is a single 2025 preprint (Voráček & Orabona); the empirical section would be considerably strengthened by including other established betting schemes (e.g., ONS, PrPlEB, universal portfolio) adapted to the horizon-aware two-sided setting.

Training details reveal substantial engineering effort (550k episodes, specific reward shaping, difficulty-matched sampling of (N, m, μ)) without ablations isolating which design choices (reward shaping, feature set, double-DQN vs. vanilla DQN, action discretization) actually drive the reported gains, limiting reproducibility of the specific performance numbers even though the appendix hyperparameters are reported.

The paper's claims of 'state-of-the-art results' in the abstract are not strongly substantiated given the narrow baseline set and synthetic-only, in-distribution evaluation; the significance of the contribution for practitioners facing real resource-constrained experiments (the motivating use case in the introduction) is therefore not convincingly demonstrated.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated theoretical framing of horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over the state (t, log W_t), with rigorous proofs using martingale concentration (Theorem 3.1) and large-deviation/type-counting arguments (Propositions 3.4 and 3.6) to characterize when Kelly, more aggressive, or more conservative betting is preferable.

The three theoretical results combine coherently into an intuitive and interpretable 'phase diagram' (Figure 1) that is subsequently validated numerically via exact dynamic-programming solutions (Figure 2), lending internal consistency to the paper's narrative.

Creative and practically relevant translation of the theoretical insights into a learned policy: a single, 'universal' DQN trained on synthetic Beta/Beta-mixture worlds that generalizes across horizons N, null values m, and distributional shapes, while preserving anytime-validity by construction (bets remain predictable and in the valid range).

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation against the only known comparable prior method (STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding) and several carefully constructed heuristic baselines (ε-greedy schedules, hedging), covering both power (probability of rejection by t) and confidence-sequence width/validity (via CDFs of lower confidence bounds), showing consistent improvements.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendices specify proofs, algorithmic implementations of baselines, DQN architecture, features, training hyperparameters, and qualitative/quantitative diagnostics (training curves, trajectory visualizations) that support the claims.
weaknesses: The theoretical propositions (3.4, 3.6) are proven only for finite-support distributions under constant-bet policies over the remaining horizon, and rely on conservative finite-T correction terms; this is considerably more restrictive than the general problem the DQN is trained to solve, leaving a meaningful gap between the exploratory theory and the actual learned algorithm's behavior.

The oracle phase diagrams in Section 4.1 require knowledge of the true PX (population Kelly bet), which is unavailable in practice; the DQN instead relies on noisy empirical Kelly/moment estimates, but the paper does not theoretically or empirically quantify how estimation error affects the correspondence between the oracle phase diagram and the learned policy's regions.

All experiments (training and testing) use synthetic Beta and Beta-mixture distributions; despite being labeled 'universal,' the DQN's generalization to qualitatively different distributions (e.g., heavy-tailed, discrete, or real-world data) is untested, so the breadth of the claimed universality is not well supported.

The empirical comparisons appear to rely on single runs/trajectories in several figures (e.g., Figure 3, Figure 4) without reported variance across multiple seeds or confidence intervals on the performance metrics themselves, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements over STaR-Bets and the hedging baseline.

The action space is coarsely discretized (half-Kelly, Kelly, all-in), and no ablation examines sensitivity to this choice or to the 22-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, which somewhat undercuts the claim of a clean, principled mapping from theory to algorithm.

The term 'state-of-the-art' is used, but the comparison set is narrow — essentially one concurrent related work (STaR) plus internally constructed baselines — rather than a broader set of established horizon-agnostic or other competing approaches, which somewhat overstates the generality of the claim.

There is no formal performance guarantee (e.g., regret bound, approximate optimality) connecting the learned DQN policy back to the theoretical phase diagram; the link is established only qualitatively via modal-action maps, which, while illustrative, is not a rigorous bridge between theory and the final deployed algorithm.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing of horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon stochastic control problem over the state (t, log W_t), which provides a principled lens (via the Bellman recursion) for understanding when Kelly betting is optimal and when to deviate.

Rigorous theoretical results (Theorem 3.1, Propositions 3.4 and 3.6) with complete proofs in the appendix, giving sufficient conditions under which near-Kelly betting is required in the interior of the state space, and when more aggressive or more defensive betting improves the probability of threshold crossing.

The theory is used to motivate a concrete practical design (3-action DQN matching conservative/Kelly/aggressive regimes), creating a nice link between qualitative theoretical insight and an implementable learning algorithm.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation: synthetic Beta/Beta-mixture/Bernoulli/logit-normal worlds, multiple ablations (action-space size, longer horizons, alternative alpha, alternative reward shaping), and real-data experiments on two distinct domains (DNA methylation, relative humidity) with explicit Type-I error checks.

The proposed procedures (hedging over epsilon-schedules, DQN policy) preserve anytime-validity by construction (predictability + boundedness of bets via Ville's inequality), so the learning-based method retains the core statistical guarantee regardless of how the policy is learned.

Comparison against the most relevant recent baseline (STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding) as well as classical empirical-Kelly and hedging baselines, with confidence-sequence width and rejection-probability comparisons.

A single 'universal' DQN policy generalizes across horizons N, null values m, and distributional families without retraining, including apparent out-of-distribution transfer to logit-normal and real data — a practically appealing property.
weaknesses: The theoretical results (Propositions 3.4, 3.6) are restricted to finite-alphabet distributions and rely on fairly intricate, conservative sufficient conditions (with finite-T correction terms) that are only verified numerically in toy examples (Examples 3.3, 3.5, 3.7); the paper does not fully characterize the optimal policy or rigorously establish the full phase-diagram picture claimed in Figure 1/2, which remains largely illustrative/qualitative for continuous distributions.

The DQN method itself is not accompanied by any theoretical guarantee beyond the anytime-validity that follows automatically from predictability; the connection between the theory (Section 3) and the specific 3-action discretization, feature engineering, and reward shaping (Section 4) is heuristic rather than derived.

Empirical plots (rejection-probability curves, CS widths) generally lack error bars or variance/significance reporting across the 5,000-trial Monte Carlo repetitions, making it hard to assess whether observed gains over STaR-Bets/Hoeffding and hedging baselines are statistically robust, especially in cases where curves are close (e.g., some real-data panels where DQN is 'close to the best' in 1/6 cases).

The two-sided adaptation of STaR-Bets/Hoeffding (originally designed for one-sided tests) is done by the authors themselves via a heuristic sign-based rule, which could bias the baseline comparison; it is unclear whether this adaptation is optimal or faithfully represents the strongest possible version of the competing method.

Real-data evaluation resamples individual observations with replacement from the empirical marginal, discarding temporal/serial dependence present in genuine sequential data (e.g., daily humidity), which is acknowledged as a limitation but weakens the practical relevance of the 'real data' claims for genuinely sequential monitoring settings.

The DQN training relies on many design choices (feature vector of 22 hand-crafted predictable statistics, specific difficulty-coupling scheme between N, m, and mu, specific concentration ranges) whose sensitivity is not thoroughly explored, raising some reproducibility/robustness concerns despite the detailed hyperparameter table.

Novelty of applying (Double) DQN to a betting/statistics problem is somewhat incremental from an RL methodology standpoint; the main novelty lies in problem formulation and the theory-guided phase-diagram interpretation rather than algorithmic innovation in the RL component itself.

strengths: The paper offers a genuinely novel framing of horizon-aware betting-based testing as a finite-horizon stochastic control problem over the (t, log W_t) state space, connecting classical Kelly-betting intuition with anytime-valid inference under a deadline.

The theoretical results (Theorem 3.1 and Propositions 3.4/3.6), while conservative, are rigorous and give complementary sufficient conditions delineating when Kelly, more aggressive, or more defensive betting is preferable, and are illustrated with worked numerical examples.

The oracle dynamic-programming phase diagrams (Figure 2) provide a useful sanity check that qualitatively matches the theoretical predictions, lending some internal consistency to the paper's central narrative.

Extensive empirical evaluation: synthetic Beta/Beta-mixture experiments, out-of-distribution generalization tests (logit-normal, Bernoulli), six real-data domains (DNA methylation, relative humidity), and several ablations (reward shaping, action-space size, longer horizons, different alpha, Type-I error checks) demonstrate a serious effort at empirical validation.

Anytime-validity is preserved by construction regardless of how the betting policy is learned, since it depends only on predictability of the bets, which is a sound and important design choice that decouples validity from the (heuristic) optimization procedure.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is narrow: Theorem 3.1 and the two propositions provide only sufficient (not necessary, not tight) conditions in isolated regimes, rely on a finite-support assumption |X|=k for Propositions 3.4/3.6, and involve loose non-asymptotic correction terms (c^+_T, c^-_T) whose practical relevance is unclear; the illustrative examples appear cherry-picked to satisfy the somewhat convoluted conditions rather than demonstrating that these regimes are common or dominant in practice.

The 'phase diagram' remains a qualitative/informal narrative rather than a full characterization of the optimal policy; the boundaries between regimes and the behavior in the large intermediate zones are not derived, only illustrated numerically via an oracle DP that itself requires knowledge of the true PX (via the population Kelly bet), which is unavailable in practice.

The DQN component, while extensively tested, has no theoretical guarantee connecting it back to the phase-diagram theory (no regret/optimality-gap bound), so ultimately the paper's practical method is a heuristic RL agent guided only loosely by intuition from the theory, not a principled algorithm derived from it.

The 3-action design (Kelly/2, Kelly, all-in) is coarse, and the 9-action ablation shows no improvement, which raises concern about whether the RL training/optimization is well-tuned (i.e., insufficient compute/data for larger action spaces) rather than confirming that 3 actions are sufficient.

Empirical comparisons lack variance/uncertainty quantification (e.g., confidence bands around the P(reject by t) curves over the 5,000 trials), making it hard to assess whether the reported improvements over STaR-Bets/Hedging are statistically meaningful or within simulation noise.

The two-sided adaptation of STaR-Bets/Hoeffding (via sign of the running empirical mean) is an ad hoc modification of a one-sided method and may not represent a fair or fully optimized baseline, potentially inflating the apparent advantage of the proposed DQN.

No code repository is provided (the 'Code:' field on page 1 is empty), which combined with the many implementation-specific choices (feature engineering, hyperparameters, reward shaping) raises reproducibility concerns despite the fairly detailed appendix.

The overall contribution combines fairly standard ingredients (test-martingale betting, Bellman/DP formulation, off-the-shelf DQN) without a new algorithmic or statistical technique beyond their combination, limiting the originality and broader significance of the work relative to its length and empirical scope.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely useful theoretical framing: casting horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over (t, log W_t), yielding rigorous partial characterizations (Theorem 3.1, Propositions 3.4 and 3.6) that formalize when Kelly, more aggressive, or more conservative betting is preferable. These results, with full proofs in the appendix using martingale concentration and Sanov-type large-deviation arguments, give real insight into the structure of the problem rather than being purely heuristic.

The resulting 'phase diagram' concept is a nice unifying narrative that connects theory to practice, and the oracle DP phase diagrams (Figure 2) empirically validate the qualitative theory in a controlled setting before moving to learned policies.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this type of paper: comparisons against the only directly comparable prior work (STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding), horizon-agnostic baselines, and a well-designed epsilon-greedy/hedging heuristic; ablations over action-space size, deadline length, and alpha; generalization tests to out-of-distribution families (logit-normal, Bernoulli); and real-data experiments on two distinct domains (DNA methylation, relative humidity) with explicit Type-I error verification.

By construction (predictable bets, Ville's inequality), anytime-validity is preserved regardless of how the betting policy is learned, so the practical/statistical validity guarantee is not compromised by using a black-box DQN — a sound and important design choice.

The confidence sequence construction and empirical CDF-based lower-bound comparisons (Figures 4-5) give a coherent secondary evaluation beyond simple power curves, and the reward-shaping experiments (Figure 6) show the framework's flexibility for different application needs (early vs. terminal rejection).
weaknesses: The theoretical results are only sufficient conditions in specific regimes (finite alphabets, particular Bernoulli examples), not a full characterization of the optimal policy; the connection between these results and the specific 3-action DQN design (Kelly/2, Kelly, all-in) is more motivational than derived, and the 9-action ablation showing no improvement raises the question of whether the phase-diagram narrative is doing real design work versus serving as post-hoc justification.

The DQN is trained on a fairly specific synthetic family (Beta and Beta-mixtures with randomized parameters); while transfer to logit-normal, Bernoulli, and real data is a strong result, the real-data evaluation relies on i.i.d. resampling from empirical marginals rather than genuine sequential real data, sidestepping potential temporal dependence issues that the paper itself flags as future work.

No discussion of the computational/training cost trade-off relative to simpler closed-form baselines (STaR, hedging), despite training taking multiple GPU-hours; practitioners may want guidance on when the added complexity of training a universal DQN is justified over the much simpler STaR or hedging heuristics, which already perform competitively in several figures.

The paper does not clearly state whether code will be released for reproducibility (the abstract page has an empty 'Code:' placeholder), which is a minor but notable gap given the heavy reliance on a specific RL training pipeline, feature engineering (22-dim state), and hyperparameters for reproducing the central empirical claims.

Some illustrative examples (3.3, 3.5, 3.7) use particular, somewhat narrow numerical choices to verify the sufficient conditions, and it is unclear how tight or representative these conditions are across the broader operating region actually explored by the DQN and real-data experiments.
